design_detail: Within-person analysis of longitudinal panel data from the Methamphetamine Treatment Evaluation Study (MATES) cohort, Sydney and Brisbane, Australia (recruited 2006–2007, followed to 2010). 469 people with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence at entry contributed up to four non-contiguous one-month windows: the month before the baseline interview and the months before the interviews at 3 months, 1 year and 3 years. Logistic models (Stata xtlogit) relate any methamphetamine use in a month to self-reported crime in the same month (any crime, drug dealing, property crime, fraud and violent crime), unadjusted, adjusted for time-varying age, income, unemployment and unstable housing (Model 1), and further adjusted for other substance use (Model 2); a dose analysis compares 1–15 and 16 or more days of use with none. The methods describe random-effects models with a random intercept and say that the fixed-effects option was used for the within-person effect (p. 3). The authors describe having applied the same within-person approach to psychotic symptoms and hostility (McKetin et al., 2013b and 2014, p. 2); the 2013 paper used the MATES cohort (card sc_mcketin_2013). The PDF (pp. 1–6) was read in full; Table 1 and Fig. 1 were checked on rendered pages. The online supplement (Table S1, crime items; Table S2, full models; Table S3, adjusted dose models) is not in the PDF and was not read.
can_establish: Within the same people with methamphetamine dependence, how much more often each type of self-reported crime occurred in months with methamphetamine use than in months without, with a comparison designed to remove stable personal characteristics (sex, heritable traits, personality, childhood adversity; fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name, see reporting issues) and with age, income, employment, housing and other drug use adjusted for as they changed.
cannot_establish: Which came first within a month (use and crime are reported for the same four weeks, and the authors say the direction could be disputed); that methamphetamine use causes crime rather than travelling with changes over time that were not measured (entering treatment, treatment received, imprisonment, involvement in drug markets, mental state); anything about people who use methamphetamine without dependence (the authors say the findings should not be generalized to recreational use); or offending recorded by police or courts (self-report only).

sample.recruitment: MATES: 400 people entering community-based drug treatment for methamphetamine use in Sydney and Brisbane, and 101 people in Sydney who were not in treatment, recruited through needle and syringe programmes and outreach services, who screened positive for methamphetamine dependence. Recruited in 2006 and 2007; follow-up interviews from 2006 to 2010, face-to-face or by phone; volunteers reimbursed up to AUD40 per interview (p. 2). The cohort's procedures are described in an earlier paper (McKetin et al., 2012), not read.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MATES: age 16 or over, comprehension of English, willingness to be followed up, and no methamphetamine treatment, other inpatient drug treatment or imprisonment in the month before entry, so that the baseline month reflected use outside treatment or prison (p. 2). This analysis: DSM-IV past-year methamphetamine dependence at entry on the Composite International Diagnostic Interview; 17 excluded for not meeting dependence criteria at recruitment, 14 for no methamphetamine use in any analysed month and 1 for declining the crime questions, leaving 469 aged 16–57 (p. 2).
sample.demographics: At baseline: mean age 31.6 years (SD 8.1); 74% male, 73% single, 82% unemployed; 87% born in Australia and 96% preferring English; median 10 years of schooling (range 6–12), 41% with a technical or trade qualification and 6% with a university degree; mean 13.3 years (SD 7.9) of methamphetamine use; 74% usually injected, 18% smoked and 7% used other routes; 84% had used crystalline methamphetamine in the month before entry, and 58% named it as their main form (base 31%, powder 8%) (p. 3).
sample.attrition: All 469 were interviewed at baseline; 379 (81%) at 3 months, 357 (76%) at 12 months and 315 (67%) at 3 years. Seven crime responses were missing, giving 1,518 person-months for property crime, fraud and violent crime, 1,514 for dealing and 1,513 for any crime (p. 2). How many people had at least one follow-up interview, and whether people lost to follow-up differed from those retained in use or crime, is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: A sample of people with methamphetamine dependence, most entering treatment and most injecting; the authors state the findings should not be generalized to people who use recreationally (p. 5). For most participants the baseline month is the month before entering treatment, which may be a period of heavier use and more crises than later months (editors' reasoning, not examined in the paper). A fixed-effects within-person estimate, the estimator the methods name, draws only on people whose crime status and use changed across their observed months: for violent crime at most the 22% who ever reported it (p. 3), about 103 people (editors' calculation), and the number actually contributing to each estimate is not reported. Losses at follow-up (a third by 3 years) may be related to both use and crime, for example through imprisonment (editors' reasoning).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported days of methamphetamine use in the past four weeks on the Opiate Treatment Index (OTI) at each interview, coded for the main models as any use in the month against none; route and main form also recorded (pp. 2–3). Self-reported abstinence was checked against hair toxicology in a subsample of the MATES cohort (n = 83; 6% false reports of abstinence), as reported in the cohort paper (McKetin et al., 2012) (p. 2). No biological verification in this analysis.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency only. Dose analysis: 1–15 days and 16 or more days of use in the month against none (p. 3). Methamphetamine was used in 61% of observed months, and 10% of participants used at every follow-up interview; in months of use the median was 10 days (interquartile range 3–20), and injecting was the main route in 80% of them (smoking 14%, snorting or swallowing 6%) (p. 3). Mean duration of use before entry 13.3 years. Amount and purity were not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Days of use of heroin, cocaine, ecstasy, hallucinogens, cannabis, alcohol and tobacco in the past four weeks were recorded (p. 3). In observed months: tobacco 90% (median 28 days), cannabis 58% (median 21 days), alcohol 62% (median 7 days), heroin 19% (median 4 days), cocaine 15% (median 2 days), ecstasy 16% (median 3 days), hallucinogens 3%; other drug use was more likely in months of methamphetamine use (rs 0.08–0.40, p < 0.01) (p. 3). Model 2 adjusts for alcohol and cannabis (0, 1–15, 16 or more days) and for any past-month cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use; hallucinogens (too few months) and tobacco are not among the covariates (p. 3). Adding other substance use to the adjustment reduced the odds ratios by a third to nearly two-thirds (Model 1 to Model 2, Table 1; editors' calculation).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: months without methamphetamine use are one of the two exposure states, by self-report (6% false reports of abstinence in the hair-tested subsample of the cohort).

comparison.controls: Each participant's own months without methamphetamine use (593 person-months) against months with use (927); no external comparison group.
comparison.matching: Not applicable: the within-person comparison is designed to remove stable characteristics (fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name; the abstract names a random-intercept model, see reporting issues).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Time-invariant premorbid factors (childhood neglect and trauma, personality, sex, heritable traits) are what the within-person design is meant to remove (fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name; see reporting issues), which is the study's central strength, as the authors say (pp. 2, 4). Not measured or not adjusted for: changes over time such as entering treatment, treatment received during follow-up, arrest or imprisonment, involvement in drug markets and with peers involved in crime, mental state (psychotic symptoms or hostility, measured in the same cohort in other papers), and tobacco use. Age is adjusted for, which in a within-person model also absorbs a linear trend over the follow-up, but not a change specific to the baseline month (editors' reasoning).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Months without methamphetamine often involved other drugs (tobacco, cannabis, alcohol, and less often heroin, cocaine and ecstasy); Model 2 adjusts for these, except tobacco and hallucinogens, with coarse categories (any use for heroin, cocaine and ecstasy).

outcomes.instruments: OTI Crime Scale, past month: self-reported frequency (none, less than weekly, weekly, more than weekly but less than daily, daily) of property crime (break and enter, robbery without violence, shoplifting, stealing a prescription pad or a car, receiving stolen goods), dealing (selling drugs to someone), fraud (forging cheques or prescriptions, social security fraud such as cash-in-hand work, using another person's credit card) and crimes involving violence (such as violence in a robbery or assault) (p. 2). The item wording is in Table S1 of the supplement, not read.
outcomes.validity_norms: Self-report, not convictions. The authors cite the OTI development study for agreement with other self-report measures, good test-retest reliability and agreement of self-reported convictions with records (p. 5); no validation in this cohort is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Each crime type coded as any against none in the past month; any crime means any of the four types (p. 3). Violent crime does not separate instrumental violence (for example robbery) from expressive violence (for example domestic assault), as the authors note (p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: five outcomes, each in three models, plus a dose analysis, all at two-sided p < 0.05 (p. 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: use and crime were self-reported in the same structured interview.

analysis.effect_sizes: Within-person odds ratios, months with use against months without (Table 1, p. 3). Any crime: unadjusted 13.2 (95% CI 8.5–20.6); Model 1 10.5 (6.6–16.7); Model 2 4.7 (2.8–8.0). Dealing: 18.2 (10.2–32.5), 15.8 (8.6–29.1), 5.9 (3.0–11.9). Fraud: 3.4 (2.0–5.8), 2.8 (1.6–5.0), 1.7 (0.8–3.3), p = 0.158. Property crime: 10.6 (6.3–18.0), 8.4 (4.8–14.5), 5.5 (2.8–10.8). Violent crime: 8.2 (4.2–15.9), 5.3 (2.6–10.7), 3.4 (1.5–8.0), p = 0.005. All other estimates p < 0.001. Shares of months with each crime, without against with use: any crime 104 of 593 (17%) against 515 of 927 (56%); dealing 6% against 36%; fraud 5% against 13%; property crime 7% against 30%; violent crime 19 (3%) against 113 (12%). Dose: unadjusted percentages by 0, 1–15 and 16 or more days of use in Fig. 1 (p. 4), with no values printed; editors' reading of the bars (pixel measurement on the rendered page): violent crime about 3%, 9% and 19% of months, any crime about 18%, 48% and 71%, dealing about 6%, 27% and 53%, property crime about 7%, 26% and 39%, fraud about 5%, 12% and 16%; the adjusted dose estimates are in Table S3 of the supplement, not read. Editors' calculation from Table 1: the raw shares for any crime are in a ratio of 3.2 (55.6% against 17.5%) and the raw odds ratio is 5.9, against a within-person odds ratio of 13.2; for violent crime, 3.8 and 4.2 against 8.2. Odds ratios comparing months within the same person are on a different scale from population-averaged or between-person odds ratios and are usually further from 1, so they should not be compared directly with those of other studies.
analysis.covariates: Model 1: time-varying age, net income in the past fortnight, unemployment and unstable accommodation. Model 2: Model 1 plus alcohol and cannabis (0, 1–15, 16 or more days) and any past-month cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use (Table 1 notes; p. 3). No covariate for interview wave, treatment or imprisonment.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the analysis was exploratory and therefore not pre-registered (p. 3).
analysis.selective_reporting: The full models (Table S2), the adjusted dose models (Table S3) and the crime items (Table S1) are only in the supplement, which was not available. The number of participants contributing to each within-person estimate is not given, and which estimator produced the printed odds ratios is described ambiguously (random intercept or fixed effects; see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not addressed formally. The authors note that few participants committed crime in months without use, which reduced robustness and widened the confidence limits, and that the dose findings rest on small numbers (p. 5). Violent crime was reported in 19 of the 593 months without use.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 469 people with methamphetamine dependence, followed over up to four one-month windows from 2006 to 2010, every type of self-reported crime was more common in months with methamphetamine use than in the same people's months without. After adjustment for age, income, employment, housing and other substance use, the odds ratios were 4.7 for any crime, 5.9 for dealing, 5.5 for property crime and 3.4 (1.5–8.0) for violent crime; fraud was no longer clearly associated (1.7, 0.8–3.3). Adding other substance use to the adjustment (Model 1 to Model 2) reduced the odds ratios by a third to nearly two-thirds (any crime 10.5 to 4.7, dealing 15.8 to 5.9, fraud 2.8 to 1.7, property crime 8.4 to 5.5, violent crime 5.3 to 3.4; editors' calculation: falls of 35% to 63%). Unadjusted percentages rose with days of use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that use was associated with significant increases in crime beyond premorbid risk and that crime is a likely social consequence of use (p. 1). The discussion calls the data robust evidence of a large increase beyond any pre-existing risk, says the time-varying controls show that the increase could not be accounted for by other substance use or socio-economic disadvantage, and says that violent crime is not only a consequence of pre-existing risk (p. 4); the conclusion calls acquisitive and violent crime likely significant social consequences of use in people dependent on the drug (p. 5). Gaps: (1) consequence is a causal reading of a same-month association; the authors themselves say the direction could be disputed, and their argument that crime leading to more use is unlikely, given the participants' long drug histories (p. 5), is not tested by the design; (2) the within-person design is meant to remove stable confounders (fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name), not changes over time: entering treatment, treatment received, imprisonment, drug-market involvement and mental state are not adjusted for, and other drugs are measured coarsely, so could not be accounted for says more than adjustment for the measured covariates shows; (3) five times more likely (p. 4) and 13.2 times more likely (p. 3) read odds ratios as risk ratios; for any crime the raw shares, 56% against 17.5%, are in a ratio of 3.2 (editors' calculation); (4) effects were dose related (abstract) rests in the article on unadjusted percentages pooled across people (Fig. 1), with the adjusted analysis only in the supplement; (5) use and crime are self-reported in the same interview; (6) the authors' own statement that the findings apply to people dependent on methamphetamine, most of whom injected, is in the limitations but not in the abstract's conclusion.

timeline.event: Within-person analysis of psychotic symptoms in the same MATES cohort, with the same four one-month windows

Within-person analysis of hostility in the MATES cohort (McKetin et al., 2014, Addiction 109, 798–806), cited on p. 2 as an earlier application of the same approach; its title, in the reference list (p. 6), asks whether methamphetamine use increases violent behaviour; not yet read
Meta-analysis by an overlapping author group, whose pooled violence estimates include the 2014 MATES hostility analysis; pooled adjusted odds ratio for violence with any amphetamine use 1.4 (0.8–2.4)
General-population birth cohort (Christchurch) sharing three authors with this study (McKetin, Boden, Foulds): adjusted odds of violence perpetration 1.60 (1.01–2.54) in periods of use
This study: within-person associations between months of methamphetamine use and self-reported crime, including violent crime (adjusted odds ratio 3.4, 1.5–8.0)

replication.where_it_stands: The within-person association between months of use and self-reported violent crime agrees in direction with the general-population birth cohort and with the within-person hostility analysis of the same cohort, but all three come from overlapping author groups and two share the MATES sample, so their agreement is not independent replication. No independent within-person study of acquisitive crime or dealing has been read for the encyclopedia; the status records the project's reading, not a search of the literature.

funding.funder: National Health and Medical Research Council (Project Grant No. 350974) and the Australian Government Department of Health and Ageing (p. 5). The role of funding source statement reads: Nothing declared (p. 5).
funding.declared_conflicts: MF and LD have received investigator-initiated untied educational grants for studies of opioid medications in Australia from Indivior, Mundipharma and Seqirus; RA has received untied educational grants from Reckitt Benckiser/Indivior and Mundipharma for studies of opioid substitution and agonist treatments in Australia; the other authors report no financial relationships with commercial interests (p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; Christchurch Health and Development Study and Department of Psychological Medicine, University of Otago; University of Queensland; University of Adelaide; University of Newcastle (p. 1). The first author was the lead investigator on the research grant (p. 5). Three authors (McKetin, Boden, Foulds) are authors of the Christchurch birth-cohort paper, and four (McKetin, Foulds, Farrell, Degenhardt) of the 2019 meta-analysis cited in the same claim (reference list, p. 6). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated short-interval measurement (weekly diaries or momentary assessment) of methamphetamine use, intoxication, other drug use and violent and acquisitive offending in people who use methamphetamine, with biological verification of use, records-based offending outcomes, and measurement of treatment, imprisonment, income, drug spending and drug-market involvement, analysed within person, so that use can be placed before or after each offence; a comparison of people entering treatment with people not in treatment would also show how much of the association reflects the period around entering treatment.

domains.note: The within-person design is meant to remove all stable confounding, the main threat in this literature (fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name; see reporting issues), and time-varying age, income, unemployment, housing and other substance use are adjusted for. Remaining concerns: changes over time that were not measured, above all the period around entering treatment (for most participants the baseline month is the month before treatment entry, when both use and crime may peak; editors' reasoning), drug-market involvement and mental state; other drugs measured coarsely; and reverse causation within the month (crime, especially dealing, can bring money or access to drugs), which the authors acknowledge (p. 5).

Self-reported days of use in the past four weeks, without biological verification in this analysis; hair testing in a subsample of the cohort found 6% false reports of abstinence. Frequency, not amount, is measured.

A sample of people with methamphetamine dependence, most entering treatment; 32 of 501 excluded (17 not dependent, 14 without use in any analysed month, 1 declining crime questions). Only people whose crime status changed contribute to a fixed-effects within-person estimate, and their number is not reported.

Most participants entered treatment at baseline; treatment received, arrest and imprisonment during follow-up are not reported or adjusted for, although they plausibly change both use and the opportunity for crime.
81%, 76% and 67% retained at 3 months, 1 year and 3 years; retained and lost participants are not compared, and missed interviews may be related to heavy use or imprisonment.

Self-reported crime in the past month, uncorroborated, collected in the same interview as self-reported use, face-to-face or by phone; willingness to disclose may vary between interviews in the same way for use and for crime, which would inflate a within-person association. The OTI crime scale was validated elsewhere.
An exploratory analysis without a protocol; the full and the adjusted dose models are only in the supplement; the estimator is described ambiguously; five outcomes in three models each.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No single domain is high, but concerns in all seven domains, several acting in the same direction (same-interview self-report, unmeasured changes around treatment entry and imprisonment, reverse causation within the month), together substantially lower confidence in the size of the adjusted associations. The design is nonetheless the strongest applied to this question in the encyclopedia's reading: comparing each person with themselves is designed to remove the premorbid differences that make cross-sectional comparisons of crime uninterpretable (fully so with the fixed-effects estimator the methods name). The study may be cited for within-person adjusted associations between months of methamphetamine use and self-reported crime, including violent crime, in people with methamphetamine dependence; not for a causal effect, not for people who use without dependence, and not for offending recorded by police or courts.

key_findings.finding: MATES cohort: 400 people entering community-based treatment for methamphetamine use in Sydney and Brisbane and 101 people in Sydney not in treatment (recruited through needle and syringe programmes and outreach) who screened positive for dependence; recruited in 2006–2007 and interviewed at baseline, 3 months, 1 year and 3 years (to 2010), face-to-face or by phone. Entry required age 16 or over, English, willingness to be followed up and no methamphetamine treatment, other inpatient drug treatment or prison in the month before entry.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1. Participants and procedure, 1st paragraph (begins in the left column)

key_findings.finding: Exclusions: 17 not meeting DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence at recruitment, 14 with no methamphetamine use in any analysed month and 1 declining the crime questions, leaving 469 aged 16–57; 379 (81%) were interviewed at 3 months, 357 (76%) at 12 months and 315 (67%) at 3 years; with seven missing crime responses, 1,518 person-months were analysed for property crime, fraud and violent crime, 1,514 for dealing and 1,513 for any crime.
key_findings.note: The 1st paragraph of 2.1 says that 469 participants met DSM-IV criteria; by the exclusions listed here, 484 met them and 469 were analysed (editors' arithmetic, 501 − 17).

key_findings.finding: Measures for the past month at each interview: crime on the OTI crime scale (self-reported frequency of property crime, dealing, fraud and crimes involving violence, such as violence in a robbery or assault), coded any against none; days of methamphetamine use in the past four weeks (OTI), with route and main form; days of use of heroin, cocaine, ecstasy, hallucinogens, cannabis, alcohol and tobacco; age, net income in the past fortnight, unemployment and unstable housing. In a hair-tested subsample of the cohort (n = 83), 6% of reports of abstinence were false.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1.1.1. Crime and 2.1.1.2. Substance use (p. 2, continuing on p. 3); 2.1.1.3. Age and socio-economic disadvantage (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: The analysis was exploratory and not pre-registered: logistic models (Stata xtlogit) with a random intercept per person, the fixed-effects option being used for the within-person effect; outcome any crime of each type in the past month; predictor any methamphetamine use in the past month; dose analysis 1–15 and 16 or more days against none; time-varying covariates alcohol and cannabis (0, 1–15, 16 or more days), any cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use, income, unemployment and unstable housing, and age (named in Table 1, notes a and b, and in the abstract; the list in 2.1.2 omits it); hallucinogen use too rare to include; two-sided p < 0.05.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1.2. Design and statistical analysis; Table 1, notes a and b

key_findings.finding: At baseline: mean age 31.6 (SD 8.1); 74% male, 73% single, 82% unemployed, 87% born in Australia; median 10 years of schooling (range 6–12); mean 13.3 years (SD 7.9) of methamphetamine use; 74% usually injected (18% smoked, 7% other routes); 84% had used crystalline methamphetamine in the month before entry and 58% named it as their main form (base 31%, powder 8%).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1. Characteristics of the sample, 1st paragraph (begins in the left column)

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine was used in 61% of observed months, and 10% of participants used at every follow-up interview; in months of use the median was 10 days (IQR 3–20) and injecting was the main route in 80% (smoking 14%, snorting or swallowing 6%). Other drugs in observed months: tobacco 90%, cannabis 58%, alcohol 62%, heroin 19%, cocaine 15%, ecstasy 16%, hallucinogens 3%; other drug use was more likely in months of methamphetamine use (rs 0.08–0.40, p < 0.01). Median net income AUD500 a fortnight (IQR 420–800); unemployed in 68% and without stable housing in 15% of months.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1. Characteristics of the sample, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Three-quarters of participants reported crime in at least one observed month (dealing 52%, property crime 45%, fraud 25%, violent crime 22%); 41% of all months involved crime (dealing 24%, property crime 21%, fraud 10%, violent crime 9%).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1. Characteristics of the sample, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Crime in months without against months with methamphetamine use: any crime 104 of 593 (17%) against 515 of 927 (56%); dealing 33 (6%) against 330 (36%); fraud 32 (5%) against 121 (13%); property crime 43 (7%) against 279 (30%); violent crime 19 (3%) against 113 (12%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, columns for months without and with methamphetamine use
key_findings.note: 104 of 593 is 17.5% (editors' calculation), printed as 17%; the denominators (593 and 927, total 1,520) are all interview-months, not the 1,513–1,518 analysed months.

key_findings.finding: Within-person odds ratios, months with use against months without: any crime 13.2 (95% CI 8.5–20.6) unadjusted, 10.5 (6.6–16.7) in Model 1 (age, income, unemployment, unstable accommodation) and 4.7 (2.8–8.0) in Model 2 (plus other substance use); dealing 18.2 (10.2–32.5), 15.8 (8.6–29.1) and 5.9 (3.0–11.9); fraud 3.4 (2.0–5.8), 2.8 (1.6–5.0) and 1.7 (0.8–3.3), p = 0.158; property crime 10.6 (6.3–18.0), 8.4 (4.8–14.5) and 5.5 (2.8–10.8); violent crime 8.2 (4.2–15.9), 5.3 (2.6–10.7) and 3.4 (1.5–8.0), p = 0.005; all others p < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, odds-ratio columns; Results › 3.2. Changes in crime during periods of methamphetamine use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Each printed odds ratio sits at the geometric middle of its interval (editors' check), so no transcription errors are apparent. The Model 1 violent-crime value is printed with a stray full stop (5.3.).

key_findings.finding: In the adjusted models, heroin use was also related to dealing, property crime and fraud, and cannabis use to dealing and fraud; heavier alcohol use (16 or more days) had a non-significant association with violent crime; none of the socio-economic indicators was significantly associated with crime.
key_findings.note: These estimates are in Table S2 of the supplement, which was not read.

key_findings.finding: Crime was more common in months with 16 or more days of use than in months with fewer (Fig. 1: unadjusted percentages of months with each crime by 0, 1–15 and 16 or more days of use); the authors report that the gradient remained after adjustment for socio-economic disadvantage and other substance use (Table S3).
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 prints no values. Editors' reading of the bars (pixel measurement on the rendered page): violent crime about 3%, 9% and 19% of months; any crime about 18%, 48% and 71%; dealing about 6%, 27% and 53%; property crime about 7%, 26% and 39%; fraud about 5%, 12% and 16%. These percentages pool months across people and are not within-person estimates; Table S3 was not read.

key_findings.finding: The authors interpret the results as robust evidence of a large increase in crime beyond any pre-existing risk, say that the time-varying controls show the increase could not be accounted for by other substance use or socio-economic disadvantage, and say that violent crime among people who use methamphetamine is not only a consequence of pre-existing risk; they add that they cannot tell whether the violence was instrumental (for example robbery) or expressive (for example domestic assault).

Limitations stated by the authors: crime was self-reported, not convictions; the direction of the same-month relationship could be disputed (they think crime leading to more use unlikely, given long drug histories and dependence at entry, and the association more likely to reflect desisting from crime during abstinence); the findings apply to people dependent on methamphetamine, most of whom injected, and should not be generalized to recreational use; few participants committed crime in months without use, giving wide confidence limits, and small numbers limit the dose findings; unmeasured factors in the same months may have contributed.

The authors state that they previously applied the same within-person approach to hostility and to psychotic symptoms (McKetin et al., 2013b and 2014); the author list includes McKetin, Boden and Foulds, three of the four authors of the Christchurch birth-cohort study of violence (Foulds et al., 2020; its fourth author, Newton-Howes, is not an author of this paper), which the introduction cites.
key_findings.locator: Author list and Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 1); Introduction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 2); reference list (p. 6)
key_findings.note: That the 2014 hostility analysis used the MATES cohort is stated by the 2019 meta-analysis (claim anchor, Results › 3.4 Violence, 4th paragraph) and that the 2013 analysis did by its own card (sc_mcketin_2013), not by this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The estimator is described ambiguously: the abstract says the within-person odds ratios came from a random-intercept logistic model (p. 1), and the methods describe random-effects models with a random intercept but say the fixed-effects option was used for the within-person effect (p. 3). The number of participants contributing to each estimate is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: If a fixed-effects (conditional) logistic model was used, only people whose crime status changed contribute, for violent crime at most the 22% who ever reported it (about 103 people, editors' calculation), so the effective sample is far smaller than 469; if a random-intercept model without separating within- from between-person variation was used, the estimates are not purely within-person. Either way the printed odds ratios cannot be fully interpreted from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says participants were five times more likely to report crime in months of use (p. 4), and the results that crime was 13.2 times more likely (Results › 3.2, 1st paragraph, p. 3); the results also say that, after adjustment, participants were five to six times more likely to report property crime and dealing and 3.4 times more likely to report violent crime (Results › 3.2, 2nd paragraph, p. 3). These are odds ratios read as risk ratios.
reporting_issues.consequence: For common outcomes the reading overstates the relative risk: for any crime the raw shares (55.6% against 17.5% of months) are in a ratio of 3.2 (editors' calculation). For violent crime, which is rarer (3% of months without use), odds ratio and risk ratio are closer (raw risk ratio 3.8, raw odds ratio 4.2; editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says effects were dose related (p. 1), but the article shows the gradient only as unadjusted percentages pooled across people and months, without values or intervals (Fig. 1, p. 4); the adjusted dose analysis is only in Table S3 of the supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose-response cannot be checked or cited as an adjusted within-person result from the article itself.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says crime was more likely in months with 16 or more days of use than for 0–15 days (p. 3), while the methods and Fig. 1 compare 1–15 and 16 or more days with no use (pp. 3–4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the comparison actually reported is unclear from the text, and the figure shows three categories.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 percentages are computed on all 1,520 interview-months (593 without and 927 with use), not on the 1,513–1,518 months analysed (p. 2); 104 of 593 (17.5%) is printed as 17%, while Fig. 1 shows about 18% (editors' reading).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; percentages may differ from those of the analysed months by a fraction of a percentage point.

reporting_issues.issue: The first paragraph of the methods says that 469 participants met DSM-IV criteria for methamphetamine dependence, but the exclusions in the second paragraph (17 not dependent, 14 without use in any analysed month, 1 declining crime questions) show that 484 met them and 469 were analysed.

The role of funding source statement reads Nothing declared (p. 5), while the funding section names the National Health and Medical Research Council and the Australian Government Department of Health and Ageing (p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably means that the funders had no role; the funding itself is as given in the funding section.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1's caption describes the bars as the percentage of participants reporting crime in the past month, but the bars for months without use reproduce Table 1's shares of months: by the editors' measurement against the gridlines (300 dpi) they read about 18, 6, 5, 7 and 3% for any crime, dealing, fraud, property crime and violent crime, which are the shares of the 593 months without use in Table 1 (17.5, 5.6, 5.4, 7.3 and 3.2%; printed 17, 6, 5, 7 and 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the bars are shares of person-months pooled across people, as the card and the claims read them, not shares of people; the caption's wording should not be cited for the share of people.
